questions.q: What is the recommended starting point for graph data modeling, per this lesson?
options: Write down the actual questions the graph needs to answer, then derive nodes and relationships from those
List every entity in the domain and make each one a node, regardless of how it will be queried
Copy the relational schema's tables directly as node labels
Start with the relationship types and add nodes only if needed later
questions.explain: This mirrors the access-pattern-first philosophy from Chapter 1 — model around the questions that will actually be asked, not an abstract entity list.

questions.q: According to the node-or-property test in this lesson, what determines whether a piece of data should be its own node?
options: Whether it needs its own relationships, needs to be queried/filtered on directly, or is shared across multiple parents
Whether it is a string versus a number
Whether it was a separate table in the original relational schema, regardless of anything else
Whether it appears more than once in the dataset
questions.explain: The concrete test is about independent identity and connectivity — not data type or simple frequency.

questions.q: Per this lesson's example, why should `orderDate` typically be a property rather than its own node?
options: It's only ever looked up through its parent Order and nothing else in the graph needs to connect to a specific date directly
Dates can never be stored as node properties in Neo4j
Because relational schemas never store dates as columns
Because Cypher cannot filter on date properties
questions.explain: Since nothing else in the graph needs to reference or traverse to a specific date independently, it fits the property side of the test.

questions.q: Why should `Product` typically be modeled as its own node in an e-commerce graph, per this lesson?
options: Many different Order nodes need to relate to the same product, and questions like 'who bought this product' require traversing to it directly
Because every piece of data in a graph must be a node
Because products are always more important than orders
Because relational databases also make Product its own table
questions.explain: Product is shared across multiple parents (orders) and needs to be queried/traversed to directly, which is exactly what earns something node status.

questions.q: What problem does using an overly generic relationship type like `RELATED_TO` for everything cause?
options: It makes queries harder to write and the model harder to reason about, losing the specificity that makes graph queries powerful
It causes Neo4j to reject the import entirely
It is actually the recommended best practice for all relationships
It has no real downside, only a stylistic preference
questions.explain: The lesson lists overly generic relationship types as a common mistake, in contrast to specific, meaningful types like PURCHASED or MANAGES.
